newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Bodies litter Zaire countryside, mission on hold.
newsitem.headline: Bodies litter Zaire countryside, mission on hold.

text.p: With a planned intervention force for Central Africa apparently in doubt, reports from eastern Zaire say the area is still swarming with heavily-armed rebels.

The United States has scaled back its commitment and Canada, the country due to lead the emergency force, said on Tuesday the mission was on hold until meetings this week clarified what was happening in the region.

Journalists in eastern Zaire said the countryside was littered with bodies of people who had been caught up in the three-cornered conflict among Zairean army troops, hardline Hutu refugees and local Tutsis.

In Ottawa, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said a political meeting on the situation would be held in New York on Wednesday, followed by a military meeting in Stuttgart, Germany, on Thursday.
"Decisions are not being made until those evaluations are finished," he said.
He said the situation was so fluid in eastern Zaire and information so fragmented that Canada and other participants needed a clearer picture to take a decision.
The U.N. Security Council has authorised a mission to get aid to the Rwandan refugees and help get them home.
More than a million Hutus fled Rwanda in mid-1994 after the country was overrun by Tutsi rebels, now in government, after the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.

On the day the mission was agreed last Friday, 500,000 refugees began a trek out of Zaire, taking a collective decision to leave their camps after the extremists who had terrorised them into staying were forced out by rebel Zairean attacks.
Grisly evidence of the terror that has rained down on eastern Zaire was found by journalists on Wednesday.
A Reuters correspondent drove into the hills behind Sake but was blocked by Zairean rebels outside a small village and ordered to turn round.
In the bush at the side of the road were the bodies of at least three people. Journalists who tried to count the bodies were told brusquely to turn round and leave.
On a road going into the Masisi region, journalists discovered a mother, father and five children who had been killed with machetes, clubs and bullets.
A child strapped to its mother's back lay with its head entirely smashed open and its brains on the road.
The entire area around Kirotshce, Minova and Sake to the west of Lake Kivu was controlled by heavily-armed Zairean rebels, some of them no more than 10 years old.

Local people said that some 7,000 people from Bukavu camp who had tried to move northwards towards Goma last week to join the refugee flow home had been blocked by Hutus belonging to the Interahamwe militia halfway along Lake Kivu.
Etienne Mahangaiko, medical director of Kirotshe hospital, 10 kms (five miles) north of Minova, said the Rwandan Hutu militiamen wanted to herd the refugees towards Numbi in the Masisi region.
"The Interahamwe wanted to go west with the refugees but Zairean rebels and Rwandan forces blocked the Masisi when the camp emptied," he said.
The suffering has continued for many of those who have returned to their homeland over the past five days.
Tens of thousands of returning refugees demanding food on Tuesday blocked the streets of Nkamira, 21 km (13 miles) northeast of Gisenyi at the border with Zaire.
The Rwandan authorities have been trying to speed them on to their home towns and villages, regardless of their state of health after the trek from Zaire.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said in a statement on Tuesday that there were "hardly any" Rwandan refugees left in Zaire and there was no need for the multinational peace force.
The French foreign ministry said there were still 300,000 refugees in Bukavu, 200,000 near Goma and 200,000 in Uvira, and the force should go ahead.
Britain followed the same line, but the United States said it was scaling down its contribution.
"This force will require considerably fewer troops than originally envisioned and will operate chiefly in Rwanda," U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said.
